definition: Replace a trivial wrapper function by using its body directly at the call sites when the wrapper adds no meaningful abstraction.
ruleOfThumb: If a function only delegates or returns a simple expression and has no independent reason to exist, remove it and use its body.

citation.author: Martin Fowler
citation.bookTitle: Refactoring: Improving the Design of Existing Code

questions.prompt: Look at this helper used in one place. What is the best first assessment about the helper?

options.text: The function can be removed and its body used directly at each call site instead.
options.explanation: This helper is a trivial one line delegate that does not express additional intent or encapsulate side effects. Fowler recommends inlining such functions to reduce indirection when they provide no extra abstraction.

options.text: The function encapsulates calculation and should be kept to provide a clear intent and future extension point.
options.explanation: Keeping a tiny function for intent can be valid when it documents behavior or will evolve. But here the body only references a constant and offers no clearer intent than the expression itself.

options.text: The function centralizes the constant and should be preserved to avoid duplicated magic constants across the codebase.
options.explanation: Centralizing the constant is important, but the constant is already separate (TAX_RATE). The wrapper does not protect the constant from duplication and can be removed without losing the centralized constant.

options.text: The function may have hidden side effects so replacing calls with the body could risk changing runtime behavior.
options.explanation: Concern about side effects is reasonable. In this example the function is pure and side effect free, so inlining is safe. One should check purity before inlining in other cases.

questions.prompt: This small formatter is used in several places. Which assessment best balances intent and duplication concerns?

options.text: Keep this small named abstraction to preserve intent and prevent duplicating the calculation in multiple places.
options.explanation: When a tiny function is used repeatedly and documents intent, keeping it avoids duplication and makes future changes easier. Fowler suggests keeping such abstractions when they express a meaningful name or prevent repeated logic.

options.text: Replace the function with its body everywhere because the calculation is trivial and adds unnecessary indirection throughout.
options.explanation: Inlining everywhere could remove a meaningful name and create duplication. If the calculation is truly one off and never reused, inlining is fine, but repeated uses favor keeping the abstraction.

options.text: Extract the constant multiplier into its own configuration and keep the function to avoid scattering numeric literals in code.
options.explanation: Extracting the constant is a reasonable refactor to improve configurability. However this does not resolve whether the function should remain; both extracting constants and preserving the function can be complementary decisions.

options.text: Consolidate the call sites into a single service and make the function private to reduce its surface area across modules.
options.explanation: Consolidation might be overengineering for simple formatting. It can be appropriate in larger architectures, but does not address the primary trade off between clear naming and duplication at call sites.

questions.prompt: Compare these two versions. Which version is better and why, given the code shown?

options.text: Version A preserves simple call sites and removes a needless wrapper that adds no observable behavior.
options.explanation: Version A avoids an extra layer of indirection that does not add intent, validation, or abstraction. Fowler advises eliminating such trivial wrappers because they increase cognitive load and call-site complexity without benefit. Keep the wrapper only if it will gain responsibility such as validation, logging, or clearer domain naming.

options.text: Version B introduces a trivial wrapper method that increases indirection without adding clear behavior or documented intent.
options.explanation: This critique is accurate about Version B, but it is the reason why Version B is worse in this context. Choosing Version B might be justified if the wrapper will provide a specific responsibility or a clearer domain name. Absent that, Version B is an unnecessary abstraction and should be removed.
